name: Grand Duchy of Moscow & Tsardom of Russia
summary: A small principality around Moscow that grew, under Mongol overlordship and then on its own, into the Tsardom of Russia. By 1700 it reached the Pacific; in 1721 Peter the Great renamed it the Russian Empire.

knownFor.label: Moscow Kremlin
knownFor.note: The fortress whose red-brick walls and cathedrals were rebuilt by Italian architects under Ivan III.

knownFor.label: Saint Basil’s Cathedral
knownFor.note: Built on Red Square to celebrate the conquest of Kazan.

knownFor.label: Streltsy
knownFor.note: Musket-armed infantry set up by Ivan IV, the first standing army of Russia.

location.value: Began around Moscow on the upper Volga; by 1700 stretched from the White Sea and Ukraine’s left bank to the Pacific.
location.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

terrain.value: Forested plains with many rivers (Volga, Oka, Dnieper) that served as trade and travel routes.
terrain.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

climate.value: Long, cold winters and a short growing season.
climate.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

resources.value: Furs (especially sable from Siberia), timber, honey, wax, grain, salt.
resources.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

disasters.value: Famine of 1601–1603 killed perhaps a third of the population; plague; frequent town fires.
disasters.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

population.value: About 6 million around 1500; about 13–15 million by 1700.
population.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; Moscow was one of the largest cities in Europe (perhaps 100,000–200,000 by 1600).
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

disease.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

migration.value: Peasants fled south and east to escape serfdom, becoming Cossacks; settlers moved into Siberia.
migration.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

economicBase.value: Farming worked by peasants who were increasingly tied to the land as serfs; fur trade.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

tradeRoutes.value: The Volga route to Persia; the White Sea port of Arkhangelsk traded with England and Holland (from 1550s).
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

wealth.value: Wealth came from land, furs and the tsar’s monopolies.
wealth.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

moneyAndTax.value: The ruble; taxes collected per household; the Copper Riot (1662) followed debasing the coinage.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

inequality.value: Serfdom was fully legalised in the 1649 law code (Sobornoye Ulozheniye).
inequality.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

governmentType.value: An autocratic monarchy: grand princes, then tsars (from 1547).
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

keyRulers.value: Ivan I Kalita. Dmitry Donskoy. Ivan III the Great (1462–1505). Ivan IV the Terrible (1533–1584). Michael Romanov (1613). Peter I (1682–1725).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

succession.value: Father to son; the end of the Rurik line in 1598 led to the Time of Troubles until the Romanovs were elected in 1613.
succession.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

institutions.value: The Boyar Duma (council of nobles), the Zemsky Sobor (assembly of the land), government departments (prikazy).
institutions.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

stability.value: The Oprichnina terror under Ivan IV (1565–72); the Time of Troubles (1598–1613); revolts of Stenka Razin (1670–71).
stability.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

eliteConflict.value: Conflict between the tsars and old noble families (boyars).
eliteConflict.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry levies of nobles; streltsy musketeers; regiments trained in the Western way (“new order”) from the 1630s.
armyAndTech.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

majorWars.value: Battle of Kulikovo against the Golden Horde (1380); conquest of Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556); Livonian War (1558–83); wars with Poland and Sweden.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

territoryChange.value: Absorbed Novgorod (1478) and Tver; crossed Siberia to the Pacific by 1639; gained left-bank Ukraine (1654–1667).
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

alliancesRivals.value: Tributary to the Golden Horde until 1480 (Great Stand on the Ugra River); rival of Poland–Lithuania and Sweden.
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

inventions.value: Cannon casting (the Tsar Cannon, 1586); the first printed books in Moscow (Ivan Fyodorov, 1564).
inventions.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

scienceEducation.value: Learning mostly in monasteries; the Slavic-Greek-Latin Academy opened in 1687.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

openness.value: Cautious towards foreigners, who lived in a separate “German quarter” in Moscow; Peter I opened the country to Western ideas.
openness.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

communicationTransport.value: Rivers in summer and sledges on snow in winter; the yam post relay system, taken from the Mongols.

religion.value: Russian Orthodox Christianity; Moscow saw itself as the “Third Rome” after Constantinople fell; the Church split (Old Believers) in the 1650s–60s.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

languageWriting.value: Russian, written in Cyrillic; Church Slavonic for religion.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

artsArchitecture.value: Icon painting (Andrei Rublev), onion-domed churches, the Kremlin cathedrals.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

socialStructure.value: Tsar, boyars, service nobles, clergy, townspeople and a large majority of peasants, more and more of them serfs.
socialStructure.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

sharedIdentity.value: Orthodox faith and loyalty to the tsar bound the realm together.
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

dailyLife.value: Wooden log houses (izba) with a big stove; rye bread, cabbage soup (shchi), kasha and kvass.

neighbours.value: The Golden Horde and its successor khanates, Poland–Lithuania, Sweden, the Crimean Khanate, the Ottomans and Qing China.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

ideasReligions.value: Orthodoxy from Byzantium; later Western technology and military methods.
ideasReligions.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

colonisation.value: Expanded across Siberia through Cossack expeditions, taking furs as tribute (yasak) from Indigenous peoples.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

riseSignals.value: Moscow’s princes collected tribute for the Mongol khans and used that role to dominate other Russian principalities.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

peakPeriod.value: Under Ivan III and Ivan IV it tripled in size and took the title of tsar.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

declineSignals.value: The Time of Troubles nearly destroyed the state, with Polish troops in Moscow (1610–12).
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

outcome.value: Became the Russian Empire under Peter the Great in 1721.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

sources.value: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia; Riasanovsky, A History of Russia.
sources.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

overallCertainty.value: Political events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia
